{"rule":"Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.","text":"The tide came in an hour early. Mara noticed when the first wave slid over the black stones below the harbor wall, swallowing the strip of sand where she had left her father’s brass compass. She hurried down the steps, boots skidding on wet algae, but the sea had already covered the place.

At the pier, fishermen were hauling their boats toward higher ground. No one could remember the water rising so quickly. The harbor bell clanged once, then again, though nobody stood beside it.

Mara found her brother Eli at the old boathouse, packing their mother’s maps into a canvas sack. He had drawn a red circle around the lighthouse on the largest chart.

“You said the light went out last night,” she told him.

“It did,” Eli said. “Then I saw someone inside.”

The lighthouse had been abandoned since the storm that took their father. Its narrow windows were dark, and the path to it was already filling with water. Mara wanted to ask why Eli had waited until now, but another wave struck the wall, sending spray over their faces.

They crossed the causeway together. Halfway across, the water reached their knees. In the lighthouse doorway, a warm golden glow appeared.

Inside, the spiral stairs smelled of salt and smoke. At the top, they found the brass compass, dry and shining on the lantern room floor. Its needle spun wildly, then settled—not north, but toward the sea.

Beyond the glass, a small boat rose on the tide. A figure stood at its bow, one hand lifted in greeting.

Mara gripped Eli’s sleeve. For the first time in years, the lighthouse began to turn."}
